newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan troops said to be pressing against UNITA.
newsitem.headline: Angolan troops said to be pressing against UNITA.

text.p: Angolan government forces appear to be set on intensifying their assault on UNITA rivals in fighting that threatens the country's precarious two-year peace, a military source said on Saturday.
The source, who spoke on condition that he was not identified, said troops loyal to President Jose Eduardo dos Santos were driving deeper into UNITA-held territory in the diamond-rich northeast.
"The Angolan Armed Forces (FAA) have built up their numbers considerably and appear determined to continue advancing south," he said.
The fighting flared three weeks ago after the ousting of UNITA backer Mobutu Sese Seko as president of neighbouring Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The dos Santos government on Friday blamed the renewal of hostilities on UNITA and said the U.N.-sponsored peace pact signed in November 1994, which ended nearly 20 years of civil war, was in jeopardy.
The U.N. military chief to Angola, Phillip Sibanda, returned to Luanda on Saturday from a visit to the northeast and will return to the area on Monday.
"The force commander visited four areas in Lunda Norte (province) on Friday and will be going back on Monday," U.N. spokesman David Wimhurst told Reuters.
"The areas he visited were quiet...he didn't hear any gunfire to suggest there were immediate skirmishes," he added.
Wimhurst said a report by Sibanda would be submitted to a joint ceasefire commission, which includes representatives from the government and UNITA, next week.

The presence of government troops and special police forces in Lunda Norte is considered a violation of the peace treaty, which states that all FAA troops are to be confined to barracks until both sides agree to their release.
Sibanda, who visited the northeast earlier in the week, said then about a dozen government soldiers had been killed and 90 wounded in clashes in the thick bush.
Relief staff said wounded government soldiers had been admitted to a hospital in the town of Nzage, one of the main centres of the region.
Military sources said the government had met stiff resistance in advancing south from Nzage into diamond areas controlled by UNITA.
The Angolan government has said it is trying to drive out armed refugees who fled the Democratic Republic of Congo during a rebel advance on Kinshasa that led to Mobutu's yielding power.
But relief agencies in Angola, prevented by the government from visiting areas beyond Nzage, say they have seen no evidence of large numbers of armed refugees.

About 46 refugees from former Zaire have been registered in Nzage, where a further 3,500 Angolans, fleeing their villages because of the fighting, have also gathered. The World Food Programme is providing emergency food relief.
An Angolan government representative said on Saturday a UNITA offer to hold peace talks in Italy was unacceptable.

Jose Ribeiro, a spokesman for the Lisbon embassy, said dos Santos had sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan ruling out any meeting between himself and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi outside Angola.
Ribeiro said the U.N. Security Council had recommended that any talks between the two leaders should take place in Luanda.
About 6,000 U.N. peacekeepers are in Angola monitoring the peace efforts that resulted in the inauguration of a national unity government, with the participation of UNITA, in April.
